name: Genistein

lead: Genistein is the main isoflavone in soy, a plant compound that resembles estrogen. It is sold as a supplement and studied in heart, bone and cancer research.
Its place in appearance discussions is as an antioxidant and phytoestrogen for skin; no trial of cosmetic outcomes has been found.

paras: It binds estrogen receptors (more strongly to the beta subtype in assays) and inhibits tyrosine kinases in laboratory tests. Oral bioavailability is described as low.
Animal studies show estrogen-related effects; human data on hormones are reported as largely reassuring by secondary sources. It is a food component and supplement rather than an approved drug.

lead: Genistein is an isoflavone, a type of plant phytoestrogen, found mainly in soybeans and other legumes. It was first isolated from dyer's broom (Genista tinctoria) in 1899 and has the formula C15H10O5. [1]

It binds estrogen receptors, with a stronger affinity for estrogen receptor beta than alpha in laboratory binding assays, and it inhibits tyrosine kinase enzymes in vitro. [2][3][4] Dietary interest in it spans cancer prevention, cardiovascular and bone health. [4][5]

In appearance and skin contexts it is discussed as a topical or oral antioxidant and phytoestrogen; no published trial located in the sources reviewed tests genistein for wrinkles, skin ageing or other cosmetic outcomes.
infobox: Soybeans, fava beans, red clover, kudzu
Dietary component and supplement; investigational in trials

paras: Soy is the dominant source, with genistein forming roughly 40-60% of its isoflavone content; fermented foods such as miso and natto contain it too. [1]

Genistein is structurally similar to estradiol and acts on estrogen receptors alpha and beta, behaving as an agonist or antagonist depending on tissue. [1][2][6] It also inhibits tyrosine-specific protein kinases in vitro. [3] Reviews of dietary flavonoids note low oral bioavailability. [7][8] A 2007 mouse study reported that genistein in the maternal diet counteracted bisphenol A-induced changes in DNA methylation in offspring. [9]

Grokipedia reports that older studies raised the question of soy lowering testosterone, that recent meta-analyses found no significant effect on male reproductive hormones, and that animal studies have shown reproductive effects and estrogen-dependent tumour promotion; these statements are secondary and unverified. [1] Soy intake and cancer risk has been reviewed in vitro and in vivo. [10]

Registered trials have studied genistein in heart failure, hyperlipidaemia and gut microbiota, transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, colorectal and pancreatic cancer, post-myocardial infarction inflammation, paediatric obesity, and Alzheimer's disease; a 400-person trial examined vascular and bone effects in postmenopausal women. [11][12][13][14][15][16][17] No studies found on cosmetic or skin-appearance outcomes.
